Every New Release on Xbox Series X Runs at 4K. Every modern AAA game released on Xbox Series X outputs at 4K resolution. THE UNSCHOOLED SAYS...
//the final result is not 4k tho. "dynamic scaling" = its not rendering a 4k image to the screen. it may output a 4k signal. thats like if i set the rendering resolution to 480p, but my gpu is still outputting a 4k image to my display, and then i say oh my pc can play games at 4k.//

Final ''Output'' Resolution Determines What You See, Not ''Internal'' Scaling Alone. When a game uses dynamic resolution scaling or AI-assisted upscaling, the final displayed image is reconstructed and output at 3840x2160 pixels, which is 4K resolution. 

Your argument falsely assumes that the original render resolution is the only thing that matters, ignoring the fact that modern upscaling techniques produce visually indistinguishable results from native rendering.

AI-Assisted Scaling Isn’t the Same as a Basic 480p Upscale. Upscaling techniques like DLSS, FSR, and XeSS don’t just ''stretch'' a low-res image like an outdated scaler, they use AI-driven reconstruction, temporal data, and frame history to generate missing details that native rendering would produce. 

Your analogy of setting a game at 480p and calling it 4K is misleading, not to mention brain dead, because modern AI upscalers ''reconstruct'' lost information to make the final 4K image indistinguishable from native rendering.

Xbox Series X Does Output at 4K. That’s the Point. The key mistake in your logic. Final resolution is what gets displayed, not internal rendering numbers. Every major Xbox Series X release outputs at 4K, whether native or upscaled, meaning the console does run all modern games at 4K resolution. 

Even if a game internally scales between 1080p and 1440p, AI processing ensures the final displayed image remains 4K, so your claim that "the final result is not 4K" is objectively false. text: I have found the RTX 4070 is really good for 3D rendering in programs like Brice, Daz studio, and the IRAY render engine, (it also rendered really fast on 3D Studio Max, but i only had an upgrade trial copy because my licensed copy of 3DS Max is a decade old and is only used for modeling).   My personal benchmark was of a scene I created specifically to punish the GPU's. I rendered the same scene in Daz Studio using the IRAY engine at 4k resolution with 4k textures on every object set for a total of 3500 iterations.   My result for the 3 cards i have were the NVIDIA 2070 Super render time 6 hours and 43 min.   The RTX 3070 was 3 hours and 22 min , and the RTX 4070 cut it down to 44 min total!!!   (I was shocked as to how fast the 4070 rendered the scene)   I made no changes to the file before rendering, so all three cards were rendering the exact scene with zero changes.   I know this was not a formal bench test, but i thought I would share the results for the 3D modelers out there since most card reviews focus on games vs 3D programs.   Hope the info helps.

text:
While I'm sure there is some high minded, 5D chess kind of reason behind how you "formulate" these things and how you suggest that even the review of the card is somehow "dreadful"... but practically speaking, the RTX 4070 is the best bang for your buck right now, and a significant upgrade for someone who is currently running an RTX 1000 or 2000 series card...

Some use cases where RTX 4070 is objectively the best bang for your buck + significant upgrade:

-you have a 4k TV that runs at 120hz but your 2000 series GPU can't do 4k at 120hz
-you have a 4k TV that runs at 120hz and HDR but your 3000 series GPU struggles with 4k 120hz w/HDR
-you are running a DDR4/PCIE 3.0 capable PC and your CPU is not a bottleneck yet
-you already have a $5k laptop with a RTX 4090 and this will upgrade your desktop significantly and saves you from building an entirely new desktop
-you aren't interested in spending more than $600 on a GPU for a minimal improvement in framerates
-DLSS is important for the games you want to play but you don't want to spend an arm + leg on an upgrade
-you understand the data, can form your own conclusions, and value pragmatism enough that youtube influencers don't have much sway over you

Power consumption differences between any mid-high range GPU NVIDIA has produced in the past 10+ years, at the end of the day, is generally a moot point that people just like to obsess over and make pedantic arguments about.

text:
Rather, it shows you how the GPU market has stagnated on design. We could be enjoying cards capable of 1440p/4k gaming at high settings/fps across the board at all skus on the product stack. But that development effort was spent on allocating GPUs for AI development. Nvidia is a trillion dollar valued company RN. Right after a pandemic where new GPUs were just not available without a 3rd party price increase (scalpers, miners, ect), and an entire product stack many people paid steep premiums to participate in. Meanwhile, Nvidia powering AI models across an entire industry, allocating silicon away from gaming cards to do it. 

The GPU market has only recently rebounded and the compounding factors turned out to be crypto currency mining and profiteering. If 3xxx series cards were true upgrades, people would not have been willing to stick with their 1xxx and 2xxx series cards for the opportunity to mine the shit out of crypto on a 3xxx series card, or try to resell it for obscene profit (sometimes they did both). 

The reality is there isn't a good reason for buying a new GPU, outside of: I want brand new (unused) and I don't have a GPU already. As it stands, there are brand new 3xxx GPUs all over the place and they are below MSRP now. These cards might perform on par with 4xxx versions in specific situations without paying that premium for newest tier. 

Nvidia should have just not released 4xxx series yet. Should have created a phenomenal product stack for an anniversary release, ensuring a true upgrade path for people. If I were buying my first card, I would rather get 3xxx than 4xxx, if I knew anything about them. That's a pretty big issue.

author: @kanjakan

text: @kanjakan  just a normal distribution/bell curve (google it). It’s pretty self explanatory when you look at it, but it’s hard to describe. It’s essentially a plot of frequency vs value. You’d have your frame rates as the x axis, same as their current bar charts, then the y axis will be what percentage of the total time spent testing was spent at each frame rate. If you had each test rig colour coded and semi transparent, then overlaid them, it would provide heaps of immediate visual information about what to expect for each setup. It would look like upside down “U” shapes with varying curvatures where the further to the right the peak is and the less spread the curve is, the better. I don’t think it requires collecting any more information than they do already.

text: Honestly, I'd love to see you use DCS as a comparison for some of these cards, simply because it's a free to play full fidelity flight sim and it would be good to see some benchmarks
author: @rshaart4810

text:
What I really like about DCS is how well it proves the point about system RAM. That game is a monster when it comes to memory. I think it was the first game to recommend 32gb, but not only that, you can see benchmarks out there for comparing different RAM speeds and timings, and the differences between bottom of the barrel 2133mhz vs 4400mhz preemo RAM kits was literally like the difference between a 6600XT and a 6800XT. That game's super sensitive to RAM apparently, and intensive af. I do like it when studios really push it to the limit, like did you know Age of Empires actually has a 2560x1440p display resolution?? Microsoft actually left a resolution for it back in the 1990s, when every screen was 640x480, pure wizardry. So I don't think it's a bad thing at all to make a game that the most high end hardware barely takes advantage of, and is why I like the overdrive fully pathtraced tech demo of Cyberpunk. I just don't like it when manipulative lying corpos then go and try to bully tech journalists for treating it like a tech demo, and not acting like it's the only performance which counts. I think I would've had a much better reception to RT in general if they'd just introduced it the way they're introducing fully pathtraced scenes, and emphasized performance otherwise. Or it's like how I was cooler receiving 3D vcache, because it's a one trick pony, so I may get 5950x anyway. Because I think the average gamer in general doesn't seem to understand not all games use system resources the same way, and DCS World vs Civ 6 vs Cyberpunk vs GTA V is a really good example of that to where you can have all kind of engine limits and resource utilizations, that make any one game not really indicative of the fuller experience, because RAM speed might not matter in lots of games, but some they do, and it's easier to make an informed choice when the answer to does it matter is "sometimes, but maybe....but those times it counts it might count a lot." Like why 5800X3D is literally superior to the 12900ks in certain titles, but other times it loses pretty badly. It isn't always that it's just "faster" or "better" but it performs differently, depending on engine and title etc.

Honestly I'm a bit shocked how much compatability there is at all sometimes. Maybe for all my bitching, it would be so much worse in tech if we had a dozen different companies. I guess it's really nice for GPU coolers, but not having standards is such a nightmare. Is why USB existed in the first place I guess. Just crazy the variety we have I guess, and how much the performance is able to vary sometimes. It's part of why the way these brick and mortar companies sadly even Steam system req sometimes is so useless, like "i5 8gb of RAM" is practically meaningless to me at this point, and RAM is definitely an area where SIs like to cheap out on. DCS is a great example why that matters.

No, they are entirely wrong here. Please stop degrading the term performance. Performance refers to ground truth updates and input latency. text:
What they don't tell you about DLSS3 on the 4070's is that it uses cores instead of dedicated hardware. That's their dirty little secret. You can tell this by the 4090 giving 2-4x frame generation, while the 4070 only gives ~1.5x frame generation. That means you're actually losing real frames to gain fake frames. The 4090 however does not lose real frames, it simply adds more frames on top of real frames. This is actually quite a deceptive change, because it means frame generation does not equally increase frame rate across different cards, making frame generation far less effective on the 4070's. If you notice on the graph, the 4070 went from 36 to 58 fps with frame generation. Since you need an equal amount of frames generated as real frames, this means with frame generation on, the 4070 is actually producing only 29 real frames instead of 36. 

That means your real-frame latency actually drops below even 30fps levels with frame generation on. This can only be explained by them secretly using CUDA cores to do the frame generation, rather than the dedicated DLSS3 frame generation hardware on the 4090. This is a big freakin deal, because it seriously undermines the benefit of even having DLSS3. I would consider this kind of deception not just borderline illegal, but actually illegal, as they have fundamentally altered the promised nature of how a core feature functions, by using real hardware in the higher tier cards, and what amounts to emulation in the lower tier cards, all without actually disclosing it.  Like a child being fed and having the spoon switched out from delicious cake to vegetables at the last minute, this is exactly what Nvidia has done with the 4070 and consumers, hoping you don't notice.

This is class action lawsuit levels of deception, like back when Nvidia made the GTX 970 with 3.5GB of VRAM, but 512MB of it was segmented from the main RAM, and thus virtually useless. The 4070 doesn't have real frame generation, it has EMULATED frame generation, that comes at the expense of core performance.

text:
DLSS3 will never justify the lack of base performance.

DLSS3 can't magically reduce input latency.  Going from base framerate of to even 2x or 3x or whatever amount DLSS3 can pull off won't matter. Your input latency won't go any lower than that of the base framerate. And this completely ruins DLSS3.  It will matter even in single player games. Imagine getting subpar performance like 30 fps, then using dlss3 to reach 90 fps, the input latency will still be as floaty as 30 fps if not worse. Reflex can only minimize the input delay, but it can't reduce it over the base framerate.


Frame generation should have always been a supplement, not a substitute to high framerate. The fact that nvidia are normalizing this for lower framerate means you're in for a sluggish gameplay experience in the future.

text:
@verakoo6187  from gpt4

When choosing a GPU for Unity development in VR, both the NVIDIA RTX 3090 and the NVIDIA A6000 are excellent options, as they offer high performance and advanced features. However, they cater to slightly different user needs.

NVIDIA RTX 3090:

    Primarily designed for gaming and content creation.
    Offers excellent real-time ray tracing capabilities.
    Comes with 24 GB of GDDR6X memory, which is great for handling large VR projects.
    More affordable compared to the A6000, making it a good choice for smaller studios or individual developers.

NVIDIA A6000:

    Part of NVIDIA's professional workstation line, designed for high-end professional use cases like scientific simulations, AI, and data analysis.
    Comes with 48 GB of GDDR6 memory, offering more memory capacity for handling extremely large projects or complex simulations.
    Features professional-grade support, drivers, and certifications, which may be beneficial for larger studios or businesses.
    Generally more expensive than the RTX 3090.

If you are primarily focused on VR development in Unity and require good real-time ray tracing capabilities, the RTX 3090 is likely the better option due to its lower cost and gaming-focused features. However, if you need the additional memory capacity and professional-grade support, or if you will be using the GPU for other high-end professional tasks, the A6000 might be worth considering.

text:
In Australia, there's already sales offers for the RTX 4070 Ti for $1199 AUD, and pricing value in pre-builts at more like $1050, so I think it's safe to say it's dipping towards $649 USD as a global price point. That makes the RTX 4070 poor value at $599 USD (AU MSRP is $1100 AUD), so I think we need to see MSRP this generation (and perhaps from now on) as an early adopter price for going early on manufacturing ramp, or as something of a price ceiling for the chip/VRAM combo sold to AIBs.

I don't like it, I don't like the margins, and I hope none of it carries over to into future generations, but that seems to be the play. Smartphones and TV pricing right now tells you that this tactic does not work long term, and it eventually drives people away from your brand. If NVIDIA had a hope in hell of maintaining this price point, the 4070 SKU should have been 56-58 SMs - i.e. an offshoot of the RTX 4080 mobile binning - and then discontinued the 4070 Ti entirely. Sadly that seems to be a trick they'll pull in a refresh instead.

text:
I love the AI stuff like DLSS, but the issue is.. you can't just turn it on in any game you want.  It has to be implemented. So until there's a method of DLSS frame generation that you can toggle via nvidia control panel, they shouldn't boast the feature as a great performance gain, when it can only be had in select titles.

Meanwhile, one of its best features DLDSR, they almost never speak of even though it makes your games look amazing but takes less of a hit than standard DSR. AND can be used in addition to DLSS for an more performant image. DLDSR @ 1.72x + DLSS Performance still looks better than native, and performs better than native too, but I feel like nvidia just ignores their really great features because they don't show a dramatic increase in performance compared to just DLSS alone.  This is why they rarely talk about DLAA either.. great image quality but takes a performance hit.  DLDSR + DLSS is basically DLAA anyway.

DLSS4 needs to offer the same feature-set, but make it widely available in games that don't otherwise have it implemented, in one way or another. At least for the frame gen aspect of it, since it doesn't require TAA, and these newer GPUs can still extrapolate the motion between two frames via hardware nowadays.

Either that or make it easier for modders to add it to their favorite titles without having to jump through hoops to do so.

text:
@Lansolot  Don't buy the bullshit on AMD's current RX 7000 series VR issues.  They are mostly solved and working great in VR at the moment (I have two friends on RDNA3 that are doing great in VR, specifically VRChat now), and I have had RDNA2 (RX 6800 XT) since launch and have always done VR with them, and the only VR issues I had were related to Windows 11 and it's launch and not AMD's drivers.  Even today, the launch issues with Windows 11 got people believing that they could avoid Windows 11 for VR, and that is another bullshit misnomer of the current state of RDNA3 in VR.

For headsets like Windows Mixed Reality, Quest 2, Valve Index, or even Vive Pro series, AMD cards have been working great in VR for a very long time... if you are talking shader issues in VRChat, then those issues were solved during Poiyomi 7.3's development when Poiyomi finally got AMD hardware and was able to fix shader code bugs that would compile and operate fine on nVidia hardware in DX11.  Those shader issues and crashes are long gone.

text:
For those of you comparing the 4070 and the 3070, and quoting inflation
Take a look at ram and motherboard prices
Take a look at CPU cooler prices.
Take a look at CPU prices
They're all dropping

Now take a look at the die size of the 3070(nearly 400mm with a 256 bit bus)
Now take a look at the die size of the 4070TI(under 300mm with only a 192 bit bus)
Now that you've slightly edicated yourself, take a look at the 12GB RTX 3060, almost the same spec as the 4070TI, its the full die, 192 bit bus, but G6 instead of G6X, still 12GB, but it had its price set in the middle of the highest inflation on CPU parts, yet it was set at only $330

Assuming the die cost of TSMC 5+ is more than 2x what they paid samsung for their 10+++, and assuming they arent getting a deal on GDDR6X, the 4070TI could have been sold at launch for $479 and maintained the same margins as the 12GB RTX 3060


The 4070TI should have been called a 4060TI and sold for $529, and the 4070 should be renamed to the 4060, and sold at $419

Honestly, i'm OK with the price being $800, as long as it was given an accurante name for its hardware class.

And before anyone argues performance class.
Thats what the 40 stands for at the beginning of 4070TI, it lets you know its the next generation, much like the model year on a car, sometimes they get alot faster/better, sometimes they dont improve at all, but at least GM doesnt try to sell you a Chevy Spark EV for $70k and tell you its a corvette "because its faster than the 1982 model year corvette"

text: If you want to dip your toes into ray traching and DLSS, and you're currently using a GTX 1080, then you should try a RTX 2060 Super or 2070 non-super. They're faster than the 1080, and a relatively inexpensive way to get access to those features. Most models also use the same single 8-pin connector that many GTX 1080 cards use, so you won't have to upgrade your power supply. My back up system had a GTX 1080 in it, and I upgraded it to a 2060 Super, and it's much more enjoyable. A 12gb 3060 is also a good choice. The three of them perform pretty similarly, so it's just a matter of whichever one you can get the cheapest. Stay away from other 2060 models, and the 3050 and 3060 8gb cards. The 128 bit memory controller hamstrings them badly.

So, RTX 4090 increased the computing speed, but the VRAM limit it can't use full performance been added. That's really bad. Because, other than those people who trying to run AI at home, why they ever need a RTX4090.

I suggest that you start by listing the tested cards lineup one by one on the screen and keep them at the same positions throughout the many different graphs. This way it's easier to listen to the video while only looking at the same area of the screen to get the compariaon you're interested in instead of trying to look at three different spots at the same time. text:
"By turning on DLSS3 Fake Frame Garbled Mess Generator".. yes... generating fake intermediate frames at the cost of input latency allows the RTX 4070 to appear to be faster than it actually is. Great... not really. It also introduces input lag and even using nVIDIA Reflex doesn't fix it. It's a gimmick. nVIDIA is getting away with snakeoil salesman-like tactics.

As for it being a topic for another video... no. People will buy the RTX 4070 before they see that other video.

It's not as good as native performance and anyone telling you otherwise should be shunned and excommunicated from society. It's a lie.

As for the 12GB Framebuffer, that's too small for $599 USD. Yes, like the RTX 3070, it looks good right now and seems to be just enough VRAM but we have all seen what has happened to the RTX 3070 as well as the 10GB RTX 3080 in newer titles.

12GB should be on a 6700XT class performer (for 1080p Ultra going forward which is a step down from 1440p ultra when the 6700 Xt released). The RTX 4070 was built for 1440p, clearly, so it should have come with 16GB of VRAM.

This is a bad product. It will need to be upgraded come next gen. The 6800 non-XT, and XT will outlive it. Mostly due to that tiny 12GB VRAM buffer. Some will call me an AMD schill but ask them to explain the current phenomenon with the latest titles spilling over 8GB VRAM and even 12GB? Just like when the RTX 3070 was released and they called me a schill then... really? It's not about the company, who cares if it's AMD or nVIDIA, but look at the VRAM sizing and the demand for VRAM from all the latest triple A titles.

The 4070 cannot be a good product when you look at the current trend in VRAM usage from triple A titles.

"That's okay I'll enable RT and DLSS", yeah... and they both require more VRAM to be implemented together. Yes, RT uses another 2-4GB of VRAM depending on the title. Common now.

text:
The thing with Arc is that it's effectively Vega 30, at least according to Chips and Cheese. It's really good when it gets loaded, hence why you'll see how the A770 competes with a 6700XT or a 3070 in TimeSpy, or how when running something stupid like Hogwarts Legacy with RT at native 4K it loses so comparatively little performance that it slumps its way to 3090 tier in some way at 23 FPS to the latter's 25 (going off of day one TPU review). The problem is that games aren't synthetic benchmarks, and most people tune their settings to match their card. So, while an A380 beats a 1060 and almost matches a 580 on Cyberpunk at 1080p Medium, most PC gamers don't want to play it at 36 FPS. So the settings go down to low, and the A380 gets around 50 FPS while the latter two get 70+.

Arc is like a random grab bag of candy you get on Halloween, and you hit up every non-normal neighborhood in town. You'll get great candy in small amounts from the rich. Someone will home make some surprisingly good chocolate. A person will slip in Tootsie Rolls with razor blades and get you in the hospital.

text: (Linus don't shadow ban me plzzz) While my takes are usually opposite of yours, and sometimes intentionally a bit antagonistic, I am trying to be thoughtful and I think I bring a different perspective that can be useful. Again, economics. I you simply can't fault a company for profit maximizing behavior, nor should anyone impose a price less than the profit maximizing one. The classic argument that profit drives innovation is still true in this case, combined with the argument that supply and demand lands on a price which is "fair". the More subtle argument, and the one I try to keep in mind is that prices are a signal. The profitability of gpus is part of what brings competitors into the market. Holding the price down is something nvidia might do if they wanted to prevent intel from breaking into the market. Furthermore, the high price of gpus implies the high value that people have for them. A tenant of economics (my perspective) is that so long as people are not coerced (I would argue gamers are not coerced into buying nvidia gpus) they only engage in transaction that is beneficial. So when people buy an "overpriced" gpu, they signal that their value for the card is higher than the price, and in fact, higher than anything else they could do with that money. As long as the cards sell, the price they set is the right one, and it reflects how people  value those cards; and imo, if you think the price is too high, you value the product lower than the rest of the market.

text:
@lucasmills1246  There's really no reason to do otherwise, I could probably still get by on an overclocked 3770k no problem. I'd even bet you some 2500k owners are doing alright. But for gaming they really set the bar for ages with the 980, pretty much anything around that level of performance like a GTX 1650 super, RX 5500XT, GTX 1060 etc is its own sort of standard, in fact the amazing thing about the new AMD APU using 780m graphics is it's comparable to a 980. So pretty much if you have a 980, or a 1060, you can run anything at 1080p more or less. Plus there's so many older games that you can even get by on a GTX 770 or a R7 270x or something provided you don't run into VRAM limits or DirectX API problems. 

I think that's part of the issue, is these companies gotta make their money, and really the vidya industry stagnated so much for so long that between nVidia normalizing shite VRAM and Intel normalizing shite++++ everything else nobody had any reason to really push the limits and just use muddy textures instead because nobody had anything that could run anything better, and so it was stuck in quadcore 4c/4t with 3-4gb of VRAM since forever ago, and so on some fundamental level it's shifted to you either come up with a gimmick like hairworks or raytracing, or you up the resolution scale. Only the resolution scale is utterly unaffordable for most people until recently, and so offering some tech demo became the thing instead. Which sucks and is sad, because of all the things I really really wanted to see improved on, it's literally the textures. That's what's been holding the industry back for 10 years. And studios really need to just leave nVidia in the dust at this point and offer high resolution at 8 gig which is new standard, and have ultra resolution taking advantage of 12-16gb of VRAM and anyone else can just drop the settings to medium to high. Because realistically, if you go on GOG or Steam like 90% of those games only are going to need 3-4gb to run at medium to high settings especially at 1080p, even good looking ones like Witcher 3 only use something nuts like 1.5gb at 1080p high settings. So I do think we're in a performance bump where fidelity and demands are going to change drastically, but a huge amount of all that also is moving towards normalizing 4k as the new standard, where 1080p is going to become like 720p is now, still playable to some people but if you're used to 4k you'll see 1080p the same way 720p looks to people playing on FHD.

text: 6:00 I do PCB design and assembly for a living, NVIDIA is not lining their pockets here - this is simply a reflection of the fact that BOM costs have doubled and tripled post pandemic due to all of the supply chain issues. For example, pre-pandemic 100x 1206 100nF bypass cap was about $0.30, now it is $0.80 for 100pcs. This is an over 2x change in price, in one of the most mass produced widely utilized components available. A single NVIDIA GPU has hundreds of these (granted in much smaller variants) - and pretty much every other component has observed similar changes in BOM cost or went out of stock completely. This eats away at profit margin, and it's not the only major concern here - The next major issue is extra redesign labor has skyrocketed for everyone now since the volatility of a BOM now means by the time the PCB is designed and in production a required component becomes out of stock, this requires stopping production and redesigning the board to account for a newer part. This is another thing that would heavily bite into NVIDIA's profit margin, frankly - i'm amazed GPU prices are as low as they are considering how much the VRAM and VRM components have skyrocketed in price.

author: @chronometer9931

text:
@chronometer9931  A 65" TV isn't designed to be used on a desktop while sitting directly in front of it like you would a 24-32" monitor. Having to sit back more than 6 feet from a display to comfortably view it automatically takes it out of the desktop space and into living space territory and beyond.

I'd wager most people would consider desktop space to encompass displays that can be viewed comfortably at roughly arm's length or closer, including computer monitors, tablets, laptops and phones. Thus his claim about 4K only being good for the desktop space makes little sense, since display sizes designed for the desktop space don't benefit from the pixel density 4K provides nearly as much as displays meant for living spaces or larger do.

text:
Hate to break facts to you, but prices don't depend on what you think they should be and certainly will never be what they were 10 years ago. 

Inflation and depreciation of money alone would make the exact same thing cost more in the future than it did in the past.

But these are not the same thing. These are way better. These GPUs aren't just marginally better; they are often 10 times, 20 times or even more powerful than GPUs from just a decade ago.

The technology has improved significantly, not just in terms of raw performance, but also safety, efficiency, cooling and so on.

We are at the level where we are literally pushing the limits of physics and cannot make the dies and transistors any smaller.

This is without even mentioning the supply chain issues caused by a literal pandemic. Till now companies are struggling to ensure sufficient silicon chips for their electronic devices.

If you actually look at the RTX 4090's performance/$ it is worth more than almost any other GPU.

The simple truth is that no one really needs a 4090. You can literally game in 8K on ultra settings and get above 60 FPS.

If you're playing at Full HD 60 FPS, even a GTX 1080 (from 7 years ago) can play most modern AAA games at high or ultra settings.

text: I hate this creep up of DLSS performance qualifying as 'real' performance. Native is real performance, that's it. The GPU will obviously perform better at a lower resolution, but I'm not paying so much for a GPU to churn out those lower resolutions trying to fool me into thinking it's something close to native. DLSS and Frame Generation should be a means to an end to achieve more performance out of cards which are slowly getting outdated and cannot perform that well years after release. Their performance shouldn't be treated as the 'standard'. It's an extra. For example, my old GTX 970 is thankful that FSR 2.1 exists because it lets it push decent frames on newer games, but that's only because it's an old gpu and this is a workaround for fps. That's all it should be. I'm gonna be really sad if settling for these shitty tactics as features for high end setups becomes the norm. Sigh. Things have changed so much.

I was interested in the 7900-XT after the price drop and because I was eye-balling that price range - a FB Marketplace listing came into view. A gentleman purchased a Red Devil 7900-XTX and then ended up wanting something else, offering it up used with Micro Center Receipt in hand for just $900.

Considering I was able to register the warranty in my name thanks to his receipt and considering the Red Devil is the best Air-Cooled AIB and costs about $1200 after tax, it was one HELL of a deal considering that according to the receipt, this GPU is quite literally 2 months old.

text:
@leonro  Power efficiency is better because they’re on a smaller/more advanced process node.  Transistor counts are doubled on the 4070 than the 3070 in spite of the smaller die, and the card is 20-30% better on average than a 3070 which does constitute a fairly substantial improvement.

DLSS3 requires optical flow accelerators which are in fact not present on Ampere.  Ampere also isn’t capable of handling opacity micromaps or displacement micromeshes. The Ada Lovelace RT core is capable of twice the number of ops per clock relative to ampere, and you also get a 50% bump in VRAM over the 3070.
